claims.text: The proposed intervention applies to single-phase high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five noble metals.
The initial state is a homogeneous solution of molecular noble-metal precursors.
Rapid heating of the precursor solution typically produces disordered precursor fragments with limited atomic mobility.
Conventional rapid heating and cooling typically causes phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and higher thermal decomposition temperatures.
An effective intermediate dwell lies at approximately 200–300 °C for about 10 minutes under an inert atmosphere.
An intermediate thermal dwell at precursor-reduction onset enhances adatom or metal-atom mobility.
The dwell synchronizes reduction of the different noble-metal precursors.
Enhanced mobility and synchronized reduction produce transient, well-mixed alloy clusters.
Well-mixed multimetal clusters nucleate or crystallize into uniform alloy nanoparticles.
Enhanced adatom mobility minimizes local concentration gradients and prevents premature phase separation or elemental segregation.
Increased atomic diffusion produces effective elemental mixing and synchronized nucleation.
The dwell steers the system toward a thermodynamically favored single-phase crystalline state, such as FCC.
Compared with no dwell, the dwell will yield a more uniform elemental distribution and a better-defined single-phase structure.
Compared with no dwell, the dwell will improve control of nanoparticle morphology.
Compared with no dwell, the dwell will reduce the thermal decomposition onset.
Structural and compositional measurements should show diminished phase segregation and enhanced ordering after the dwell.
The intervention requires the precursor reduction kinetics to overlap within approximately 200–300 °C.
Below the applicable thermal window, atomic mobility will be insufficient, whereas more severe dwell conditions can cause particle coarsening.
The dwell must be calibrated to avoid secondary-phase formation and significant particle coarsening.
